verses.text: Now Joab the son of Zeruiah perceived that the king’s heart was toward Absalom.

Joab sent to Tekoa, and brought a wise woman from there, and said to her, “Please act like a mourner, and put on mourning clothing, please, and don’t anoint yourself with oil, but be as a woman who has mourned a long time for the dead.
Go in to the king, and speak like this to him.” So Joab put the words in her mouth.
When the woman of Tekoa spoke to the king, she fell on her face to the ground, showed respect, and said, “Help, O king!”
The king said to her, “What ails you?” She answered, “Truly I am a widow, and my husband is dead.
Your servant had two sons, and they both fought together in the field, and there was no one to part them, but the one struck the other, and killed him.

Behold, the whole family has risen against your servant, and they say, ‘Deliver him who struck his brother, that we may kill him for the life of his brother whom he killed, and so destroy the heir also.’ Thus they would quench my coal which is left, and would leave to my husband neither name nor remainder on the surface of the earth.”
The king said to the woman, “Go to your house, and I will give a command concerning you.”
The woman of Tekoa said to the king, “My lord, O king, may the iniquity be on me, and on my father’s house; and may the king and his throne be guiltless.”
The king said, “Whoever says anything to you, bring him to me, and he will not bother you any more.”

Then she said, “Please let the king remember Yahweh your God, that the avenger of blood destroy not any more, lest they destroy my son.” He said, “As Yahweh lives, not one hair of your son shall fall to the earth.”
Then the woman said, “Please let your servant speak a word to my lord the king.” He said, “Say on.”

The woman said, “Why then have you devised such a thing against the people of God? For in speaking this word the king is as one who is guilty, in that the king does not bring home again his banished one.
For we must die, and are like water spilled on the ground, which can’t be gathered up again; neither does God take away life, but devises means, that he who is banished not be an outcast from him.

Now therefore seeing that I have come to speak this word to my lord the king, it is because the people have made me afraid. Your servant said, ‘I will now speak to the king; it may be that the king will perform the request of his servant.’
For the king will hear, to deliver his servant out of the hand of the man who would destroy me and my son together out of the inheritance of God.
Then your servant said, ‘Please let the word of my lord the king bring rest; for as an angel of God, so is my lord the king to discern good and bad. May Yahweh, your God, be with you.’”
Then the king answered the woman, “Please don’t hide anything from me that I ask you.” The woman said, “Let my lord the king now speak.”

The king said, “Is the hand of Joab with you in all this?” The woman answered, “As your soul lives, my lord the king, no one can turn to the right hand or to the left from anything that my lord the king has spoken; for your servant Joab urged me, and he put all these words in the mouth of your servant;
to change the face of the matter has your servant Joab done this thing. My lord is wise, according to the wisdom of an angel of God, to know all things that are in the earth.”
The king said to Joab, “Behold now, I have done this thing. Go therefore, and bring the young man Absalom back.”

Joab fell to the ground on his face, showed respect, and blessed the king. Joab said, “Today your servant knows that I have found favor in your sight, my lord, king, in that the king has performed the request of his servant.”
So Joab arose and went to Geshur, and brought Absalom to Jerusalem.
The king said, “Let him return to his own house, but let him not see my face.” So Absalom returned to his own house, and didn’t see the king’s face.
Now in all Israel there was no one to be so much praised as Absalom for his beauty. From the sole of his foot even to the crown of his head there was no defect in him.

When he cut the hair of his head (now it was at every year’s end that he cut it; because it was heavy on him, therefore he cut it); he weighed the hair of his head at two hundred shekels,  after the king’s weight.
Three sons were born to Absalom, and one daughter, whose name was Tamar. She was a woman with a beautiful face.
Absalom lived two full years in Jerusalem, and he didn’t see the king’s face.
Then Absalom sent for Joab, to send him to the king, but he would not come to him. Then he sent again a second time, but he would not come.
Therefore he said to his servants, “Behold, Joab’s field is near mine, and he has barley there. Go and set it on fire.” So Absalom’s servants set the field on fire.
Then Joab arose, and came to Absalom to his house, and said to him, “Why have your servants set my field on fire?”

Absalom answered Joab, “Behold, I sent to you, saying, ‘Come here, that I may send you to the king, to say, “Why have I come from Geshur? It would be better for me to be there still. Now therefore let me see the king’s face, and if there is iniquity in me, let him kill me.”’”
So Joab came to the king, and told him; and when he had called for Absalom, he came to the king, and bowed himself on his face to the ground before the king; and the king kissed Absalom.

footnotes.content: Joab sees what David won't admit—the king's heart pulls toward Absalom despite his banishment. How many times the Lord has sent servants to read what our hidden hearts long for, to gently call us toward reconciliation.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A wise woman from Tekoa, sent to play a part in the king's own heart's healing. Joab knows what to ask of her—put on sorrow like a garment, let mourning speak where words would fail. The Lord works through unexpected vessels.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joab puts the words in her mouth—a small deception in service of truth. The woman becomes a messenger of something David needs to hear about mercy and the bonds that hold a kingdom together.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: She falls on her face before the king, speaks through gesture what her words will soon plead. Desperation kneels before power, trusting that mercy lives in a king's heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king asks what troubles her. A widow, a woman stripped of her husband's protection—she speaks her loss plainly, inviting the king into her loneliness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Two sons quarreled in an empty field, and now one is dead by the hand of the other. No one was there to separate them, to speak peace between brothers. How the Lord grieves when kin become enemies.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The family demands justice—surrender the son who struck his brother so they can kill him. But she speaks the heart's real terror: they would destroy the heir, leave her husband's name erased from the earth. This is the old custom of blood vengeance, and it devours families whole.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king hears her cry and offers what a king offers—'Go home, and I will command concerning you.' A glimmer of hope in her darkness; the king will act.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: She bows even deeper, calling the weight of her sin upon her own head and her father's, that the king and his throne remain guiltless. She shields the king from her need, even as she pleads.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king promises protection: whoever troubles her will answer to him. His power stands as a shield around her. Sometimes the arm of authority that we fear is the same arm that guards the helpless.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: She invokes the Lord's name—'Remember Yahweh your God.' The king swears by Yahweh's life that not a hair of her son shall fall. She has called the king's own faith into the room, and he answers with an oath.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: She asks leave to speak once more. The king, now softened by her story, gives her the floor. In small mercies we see how grace opens a door to deeper truth.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Now she pivots—'Why then have you devised such a thing against the people of God?' She speaks to the king as if he were judging against God's own family. His refusal to bring Absalom home mirrors his judgment against his own banished son.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: We must die; we are like water spilled and cannot be gathered up. Yet God does not take away life but devises means that the banished not be cast out from him. The woman speaks a theological truth: mercy and restoration are God's way, not death and exile.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: She reveals her motive: the people sent her in fear. Not she alone, but the whole kingdom grieves the breach between father and son. She speaks on behalf of a people that longs for wholeness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: She begs the king to deliver her and her son from the hand of the avenger—out of the inheritance of God. Even in her invented tale, she speaks the deeper truth: we are God's inheritance, and He does not abandon what belongs to Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: She calls the king 'as an angel of God' who discerns good from evil. The flattery carries a truth: a just king, like the Lord's messenger, brings peace and reconciliation.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David sees through her now—he asks her to hide nothing. The question is not whether she was sent, but whether the word she spoke was true. Truth can come through an instrument, even a false one.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: She confesses: Joab put the words in her mouth. The king can turn neither right nor left from what he has said, she means—his own oath binds him. A servant speaks what the master can no longer deny.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: She names Joab's purpose: to change the face of the matter. The king's wisdom, like an angel of God, discerns all things in the earth. Even beneath a deception, David recognizes what his own heart has needed to hear.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king yields at last: 'I have done this thing.' Go, bring young Absalom back. A word speaks what the heart could not before—the king's wall of anger begins to crack.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joab falls on his face, blesses the king, knowing he has found favor. The servant sees his master's heart before the master himself fully knows it. Mercy often arrives dressed as a favor.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joab goes to Geshur, to the place where Absalom had fled after Amnon's death, and brings him home to Jerusalem. The prodigal's journey begins at last.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: But the king's grace has a limit: 'Let him return to his own house, but let him not see my face.' Absalom is home, yet banished still. Reconciliation remains incomplete—a door cracked open, but not yet fully turned on its hinges.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: All Israel praises Absalom's beauty—from sole of foot to crown of head, no defect in him. His outward loveliness is unmatchable. Yet a beautiful face can hide a restless, ambitious heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Once each year he cut his hair—it was heavy upon him—and weighed it at two hundred shekels by the king's weight. The detail marks his distinction: even his hair measures in the king's standard, a reminder of his place and his burden.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Three sons and a daughter named Tamar were born to him while in exile, living in the land of Geshur. Even separated from his father, Absalom builds a house. His children carry his name forward.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Two full years in Jerusalem, and still he does not see his father's face. Allowed to return, but not to reconcile. A home that is not home—walls around him, yet no father's embrace.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Absalom tries to summon Joab, the man who brought him home, perhaps hoping he will help bridge the final distance to his father. But Joab will not come. The door that opened grows cold again.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In frustration, Absalom tells his servants to set Joab's barley field on fire. A young man's impatience burns what might have been a bridge. Anger speaks louder than patience.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joab comes at last, demanding why his field has been burned. The fire has forced what courtesy would not—a confrontation, a moment of consequence for Absalom's impatience.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Absalom tells Joab his heart: he was sent to the king to ask, 'Why have I come from Geshur? It would be better to be there still. Let me see the king's face, or let him kill me.' The young man speaks his desperation plainly—exile or death, but not this limbo.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joab brings Absalom's words to the king, and the king calls for him. Absalom bows low before his father, and the king kisses him. Readers today hear an echo in that kiss—grace restores what anger had broken, and a father's arm opens once more. As of 2026-10, we still see in this the mercy that turns a face back toward home.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
